summary: Asks for the character set koi8-r, used for Cyrillic text on Unix systems and networks in the former Soviet Union, to be registered. The memo argues that its large user community makes registration worthwhile, even though it is not an international standard.

eli5.summary: Different countries use different alphabets. This memo asks to put a popular way of writing Russian letters on the official list so computers can agree on it.

questions: cyrillic character set for internet mail
how to send russian text in email
subtitle: Standardizing a widely-used encoding for Cyrillic text.

tldr.problem: Different parts of the internet were using koi8-r to send Cyrillic text, but it was not officially registered as a standard character set.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC requests formal registration of koi8-r as a MIME character set, with a mapping table showing how each byte corresponds to Unicode characters.
tldr.outcome: Registration enables mail systems to reliably agree on how to send and display Russian and other Cyrillic text across networks.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: Unix systems in former Soviet Union

today: RFC 1489 registered koi8-r as an official MIME character set, allowing email systems to handle Cyrillic text reliably. The standard remains in use for legacy systems and specific use cases, though UTF-8 and other Unicode-based encodings have become more common for international text.

sections.title: A Widely-Used Encoding Without Official Status
sections.content: The koi8-r character set was already the de-facto standard for Cyrillic text on Unix systems and networks in the former Soviet Union, with a large user community including RELCOM Net. However, it had never been officially registered. The Society of Unix User Groups (SUUG) argued that its widespread use justified formal registration as a MIME character set.
sections.eli5: One way of writing Russian letters was already popular, but nobody had written it down officially.

sections.title: The koi8-r Encoding
sections.content: Koi8-r is an 8-bit character set where the lower 128 bytes are pure ASCII, and the upper 128 bytes map to Cyrillic letters, graphics characters, and special symbols. The RFC includes a C language table mapping the upper half to Unicode (ISO 10646), showing that byte 0xC0 represents Cyrillic small letter yu, for example. The encoding combines elements from GOST 19768-74 (old-koi8), ISO 6937/8, and other published standards.
sections.eli5: The first half of the encoding is just regular English letters. The second half maps to Russian letters and special symbols.

sections.title: Character Descriptions
sections.content: The RFC provides detailed descriptions of all 128 characters in the upper half, organized by their Unicode values. These include Cyrillic capital and small letters (from IU down to HARD SIGN), box-drawing characters (FORMS LIGHT HORIZONTAL, DOUBLE VERTICAL, etc.), and mathematical symbols (LESS THAN OR EQUAL TO, SQUARE ROOT, DIVISION SIGN). This comprehensive table ensures that any system implementing koi8-r can map correctly to Unicode.
sections.eli5: There is a detailed list saying which number stands for which letter or symbol.
